slides.title: Why we need tokens
slides.summary: Machines can't read text, only numbers. A tokenizer turns your text into numbers so the model can work with it.
body: Machines can't read text. They only understand numbers. So before anything else, your text has to be turned into numbers. The tool that does this is called a tokenizer.

Every tokenizer has its own vocabulary: a fixed list of pieces of text, where each piece has a number. The pieces are called tokens, and their numbers are token IDs. For example, "␣learning" (with its leading space) might be token 6975, as in the diagram below.

The tokenizer is a simple algorithm. It reads your text from left to right, finds the longest piece it knows from its vocabulary, and swaps that piece for its token ID. Then it does the same with the rest of the text.

Text goes in, and a list of token IDs comes out.

• It's trained once, on its own, before the model. Then its vocabulary is locked, and the model learns one vector for each entry.

• It doesn't care about meaning. It only splits text into pieces it has seen often. Working out what those pieces mean is the model's job, later.

figure.alt: The sentence "I am learning tokenization" goes into a tokenizer, which checks a fixed vocabulary of about 128,000 pieces. It splits the text into five tokens: I, am, learning, token and ization, with the last word split in two. Each token becomes its row number in the vocabulary, so the model reads the list 40, 1097, 6975, 4037, 2065.
figure.caption: The whole journey in one picture: text goes in, the tokenizer splits it using the vocabulary, and the model only ever sees the ID numbers.

slides.title: How big should a token be?
slides.summary: Tokens could be single letters, whole words or parts of words. Every modern model uses parts of words.
body: A tokenizer could split text into pieces of any size. There are three choices:

ul: Single letters: a tiny vocabulary, but every word turns into many tokens. Texts get long, and long texts make the model much slower (see Attention).
Whole words: short texts, but you'd need millions of entries, and any typo, name or new word would be unknown.
Parts of words: the middle ground everyone uses. Common words like "the" get one token. Rare words are built from common pieces: "unbelievable" becomes "un" + "believ" + "able".

body: <mark>Parts of words keep the vocabulary a manageable size while still being able to build any word.</mark>

slides.title: Raw bytes: how modern tokenizers start
slides.summary: Underneath every letter is a list of small numbers called bytes. Modern tokenizers start from those, so no text is ever unknown.
body: Computers don't store letters. They store text as bytes: small numbers from 0 to 255. A standard called UTF-8 says which bytes stand for which character:

ul: Plain English letters take 1 byte each: A is 65.
Accented letters take 2: é is 195 169.
Many other scripts take 3: the Hindi letter न is 224 164 168.
Emoji take 4: 😀 is 240 159 152 128.

body: A byte-level tokenizer starts with all 256 possible byte values as its first 256 tokens. Because every possible text is made of bytes, nothing is ever "unknown": rare characters just use more tokens.

Training (BPE, on the next slide) then joins bytes that often appear together into bigger tokens. Common English words end up as a single token, while a rare emoji may stay as 4 separate byte tokens. GPT-2 popularised this approach in 2019; OpenAI's tiktoken works this way, and tokenizers built with SentencePiece fall back to bytes for anything they don't know.

body.note: In code: new TextEncoder().encode("é") gives [195, 169]. That list of numbers is what a byte-level tokenizer starts from.

viz.html: Each box is one character, with its UTF-8 bytes underneath. Amber boxes need more than one byte. Try another language, or add emoji.

slides.title: How BPE builds the vocabulary
slides.summary: BPE builds a vocabulary by repeatedly joining the most common pair of neighbouring pieces.
body: Byte pair encoding (BPE) began as a way to compress files. Tokenizers use it because it finds the pieces that are common in real text by itself, without any grammar rules.

ul: Start with every word split into single bytes (shown here as letters).
Count how often each pair of neighbouring pieces appears in all the training text.
Join the most common pair into a new piece, and save that join as a rule.
Repeat until the vocabulary is big enough, usually 50,000 to 200,000 pieces.

body: Click Apply next merge. e and s sit next to each other most often, so they become es. Then es + t becomes est, and so on.
To split new text, break it into bytes and replay the saved joins in the same order. <mark>The same text always gives the same tokens.</mark>

body.note: The tokenizer is trained once, on its own, before the model. Then its vocabulary is locked, and the model learns one vector for each entry.

slides.title: Try a tokenizer
slides.summary: Play with a tokenizer to see why the number of tokens doesn't match the number of words.
body: This is a toy tokenizer that knows about 100 pieces. At each point in the text, it grabs the longest piece it knows. Real tokenizers like OpenAI's tiktoken and Google's SentencePiece know 50,000–200,000 pieces and use learned rules, but they behave in the same way.
Things to try:

ul: Misspell a word, like artifical. The tokenizer knows "artificial" as one piece, but the typo breaks into several smaller ones.
Remove the space before a word. The space in front is usually part of the token, so ␣learning and learning have different IDs and mean slightly different things to the model.
Type in another language. Pieces the vocabulary doesn't have fall back to single letters. So non-English text often needs more tokens to say the same thing, which also makes it cost more.

body.note: Because the model sees chunks, not letters, some easy-looking tasks trip it up. The next slide shows the most famous one.

viz.html: Small grey numbers are made-up token IDs. ␣ marks a leading space.

slides.title: The strawberry problem: why counting letters is hard
slides.summary: Ask "How many r's in strawberry?" and many models used to say 2. The reason is tokens: the model never sees the letters.

ul: The model doesn't see letters. It sees "strawberry" as two or three chunks, like str · aw · berry.
Each chunk is just a number to it. The r's are hidden inside those numbers.
Answering straight away, it has to guess. "2" sounds right, because "berry" has two r's.

body.h: How modern models get it right

ul: Spell it out first. Reasoning models write s-t-r-a-w-b-e-r-r-y before answering. Each letter becomes its own token, so now every r is visible and can be counted.
Or use a tool. Running "strawberry".count("r") in code gives exactly 3.

body: <mark>Spelling a word out turns letters the model can't see into tokens it can read.</mark>

body.note: The same blind spot affects any task that needs the letters inside a token: spelling a word backwards, counting characters, or finding words that start with a given letter.

viz.html: Switch between the three views, then step through how a reasoning model counts. The split and IDs are illustrative; real tokenizers differ.

figure.alt: You see the ten letters s t r a w b e r r y, with three r's. The model sees three tokens instead, str, aw and berry, which reach it only as the numbers 496, 675 and 15717, so the letters are hidden. Answering straight away, it guesses 2, because berry has two r's. Spelling the word out first, one letter per token, lets it count the r's one by one and answer 3.
figure.caption: The whole problem in one picture: the letters are there for you, but hidden from the model unless it spells them out.

slides.title: Special tokens and chat templates
slides.summary: A chat is turned into one long line of tokens, with special tokens marking who is speaking.
body: Some vocabulary entries never come from normal text. These special tokens are signals the model learned in training: start of text, end of text, padding, and markers for each speaker in a chat (system, user, assistant).

A chat API takes your list of messages and lays them out using a chat template: every message in order, wrapped in speaker markers, as one long line of tokens. The model then writes the assistant's reply right after the last <|assistant|> marker.

ul: The system prompt isn't a separate input. It's just the first tokens in the line.
Each model family has its own template. Use the wrong one and the quality drops a lot, because the model never saw that format in training.
<mark>Good serving code turns a typed "<|user|>" into ordinary letters, not the special token, so a user can't pretend to be someone else.</mark>

body.note: It's like an HTTP request being turned into bytes to send over the network. The API gives you neat, structured messages; the model only ever sees the flattened version.

slides.title: The context window: a limit counted in tokens
slides.summary: A model can only look at a fixed number of tokens at once. That limit, the context window, is one big reason token counts matter.
body: Every model has a context window: the most tokens it can handle in one request. Everything has to fit inside it: the system prompt, the whole chat so far, any documents you attach, and the reply it's writing.

ul: Sizes have grown fast. GPT-2 (2019) could handle 1,024 tokens. Many models today take 128,000, and some over 1,000,000.
Roughly: 1,000 tokens is about 750 English words, so 128,000 tokens is about a 300-page book.
The reply counts too. The tokens the model writes come out of the same window, and there's usually a separate cap on how long one reply can be.

body: <mark>When a chat gets too long, something has to give: the app drops or summarises the oldest messages, or the request is rejected. Anything dropped is simply gone as far as the model is concerned.</mark>

body.note: This is where tokenization hits you in practice. Text that needs more tokens, like some languages or messy formatting, fills the window faster and costs more. How the model uses the window, and why long contexts are slow, comes in Output & inference.

viz.html: Token counts are rough. Real apps also reserve room for tool results and the model's thinking.

slides.title: Why tokens cost money
slides.summary: AI companies charge by the token, because every token takes computing power. More tokens means a bigger bill and a slower answer.
body: Every token the model reads or writes runs through billions of numbers on expensive GPUs. So providers charge by the token, usually as a price per million tokens.

ul: Input tokens are what you send: the system prompt, the chat so far, any documents. They're cheaper, because the model reads them all at once.
Output tokens are what it writes. They usually cost 4 to 5 times more, because each one needs its own run through the whole model.
The whole chat is sent every time. The model has no memory, so each new question re-sends all the earlier messages. A long chat gets more expensive with every turn.
Thinking counts too. Reasoning models are billed for their hidden thinking, as output tokens.

body: <mark>You pay for every token in and every token out, so long prompts, long chats and long answers all add up.</mark>

ul: Reuse the same opening. With prompt caching, a long system prompt that stays the same is billed at a big discount after the first time.
Send only what's needed. Trim old messages and include just the relevant parts of documents.
Match the model to the job. A small model is often 10 times cheaper and fine for simple tasks.
Cap the reply length when you only need a short answer.

body.note: English averages about 0.75 words per token. Many other languages need more tokens to say the same thing, so the same message can cost more.

viz.html: Example prices, roughly in line with typical 2025 list prices. Real prices vary by provider and change often.
